translations.text: On Fasting, Chapter 2

"Comfort the people, you priests; speak into the ears of Jerusalem": this is the word of the prophet, and it is enough to increase the zeal of the diligent and to make the negligent and slack diligent.
For this reason commanders too, when they lead the people into battle, use words of encouragement toward them before the battle.
And such words have such power that many even come to despise death because of them.
And the trainers of wrestlers and the instructors of athletes, when they lead those athletes to the contest, say much to them and strengthen them in endurance for the sake of winning the crown.
Because of their many words, and out of desire for victory, they have disregarded their own bodies.
For this reason, then, the word of encouragement is fitting for me as well,
I who am drawing up the soldiers of Christ for battle against invisible enemies, and who through fasting am preparing the contestants of holiness for the crowns of righteousness.
And what shall I say, brothers? For I say this: that those who train in human soldiering and who contend hard [?] in the battles of this world
need to fatten themselves with an abundance of foods, so that they may stand up more strongly against battles and endure hardships.
But those whose "struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities and powers and the world-rulers of this darkness,
against the evil spirits": it is good for them to train themselves for that battle through fasting and ascetic struggle.
For as oil makes the athlete sleek, so fasting strengthens the contestant of holiness; for however much you take away from the body,
by so much will you make the soul shine with spiritual delight. For it is not by bodily strength but by courage of soul and endurance of hardships that victory over those invisible enemies is won.
Fasting, then, is always and at every time a benefit to those who practice it,
for neither does the warfare of the devil overcome the one who fasts, and moreover those angels who guard our life stay more steadfastly with those whose souls have been purified by fasting.
But fasting is especially good now, when its proclamation has gone out into all the world.
And neither region, nor village, nor city, nor a single nation, nor even the farthest places of the earth have been left
without having heard this proclamation; rather, soldiers and travelers and sailors and merchants, all alike, hear this proclamation and receive it with joy.
Therefore let no one exclude himself from the ranks of those who fast, in which all nations and every age and all distinctions of rank are counted.
It is angels who register those who fast in all the churches.

See that you do not, for a small craving for food, lose that registration by the angel and bring it on yourself that the one who registers the soldiers should write you down among those missing from the ranks.
It is a lighter thing for someone to be found in battle defeated, abandoning his weapons and fleeing, than to be shown as one who has thrown away that great weapon, fasting.
If you are rich, do not despise fasting, and do not consider it unworthy to be your table-companion and to be brought to your table,
and do not send it away from your house unhonored and despised because of your desires,
lest it accuse you before the Lawgiver of fasts and complain about you, and often bring upon you the judgment of want, either through sickness of the body or through some other grievous trial.
Let the poor man not be negligent toward fasting, for he has had it from the very beginning as his housemate and table-companion.
For women, fasting is as proper and natural as breathing. Let children, like tenderly tended plants, be watered with the water of fasting.
For the old, being accustomed to it from early on lightens the labor, for labors trained by long habit seem less burdensome.
For experienced travelers, again, fasting is a fellow traveler who runs well, for just as luxury weighs them down
when they carry a load of many foods, so fasting makes them light and free of weariness.
Then again, understand this too: when the soldiers of this world are ordered to march far away on campaign,
they take with them not delicacies but necessary food, without which they cannot survive.
But we, who go out to fight the invisible enemies, and to whom, after victory over them, ascent to the heavenly homeland is granted,
should we not all the more constrain ourselves and be content with only what nature needs, and not seek delicacies and luxury?
Endure hardship as a good soldier and contend well, that you may be crowned, for you know that every contestant always fasts.
And let this also be known: for the soldiers of this world, the ration increases in proportion to their labors;
but among the spiritual soldiers, the one who has the least food has the greater honor.
For just as this helmet of ours differs by nature from the corruptible one, since the material of their helmet is bronze, while ours is fashioned from the hope of salvation;
and their shield is made of wood and hide, while to us has been given the shield of faith;
and again we are girded with the mail of righteousness, while they bear a kind of tunic made of iron chains;
and to us has been given the sword of the Spirit for battle, while they draw the sword of iron, so too, then, the food is not one and the same
that strengthens both us and them: rather, divine teachings strengthen us, while what they desire is the filling of the belly.
Since, then, this turning of the year has brought us to these longed-for days, as to those who nurtured us,
let us therefore receive with joy these days, through which the Church has given us birth unto holiness.
Therefore, when you fast, do not be gloomy in the Jewish manner, but according to the word of the Gospel make your head shine;
do not mourn over the want of the belly, but rejoice over spiritual good things, for you know that "the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh."
Since, then, these are opposed to one another, let us therefore diminish the luxury of the flesh and increase the strength of the soul,
so that through fasting we may become victors over the passions and put on the crowns of victory.
From now on prepare yourself, so that you may be worthy to receive that honorable fast.
Do not corrupt tomorrow's fast with today's drunkenness. This is an evil device and this thought is vain:
that since a fast of few days has been proclaimed to us, we should darken ourselves with drunkenness today.
For no one who intends to be united with an honorable woman by the law of marriage would first join himself to harlots and defiled women,
for the lawful wife will not tolerate living together with those corrupted women.
And you too, then, when you are awaiting the fast, do not bring in beforehand drunkenness, that notorious harlot, the mother of shamelessness, that lover of laughter,
that crafty one, ready for every kind of indecency; for prayer and fasting will not enter into a soul defiled by drunkenness.
The Lord receives the one who fasts within those places of holiness, but the drunkard, as one defiled and unclean, he does not receive.
For if you come tomorrow stinking of stale wine, how shall I count that drunkenness of yours as fasting?
For do not say this, that only at that hour you have not drunk, but understand this, that you are unclean from wine. Among whom shall I count you?
Among the drunkards or among those who fast? The drunkenness of the day before draws you to itself; the abstinence from food of that hour testifies to your fasting.

You are in doubtful standing because of drunkenness, like a captive, and you cannot rightly escape slavery, for there is on you a clear sign of slavery: the stench of drunkenness that has remained on you.
Indeed, the first day of the fast will be useless and unapproved for you, for the portions and remnants of drunkenness are still with you,
and that whose beginning is unapproved is useless in its entirety, for "drunkards shall not inherit the kingdom of heaven."
If you come to the fast drunk, what profit is it to you? For if drunkenness casts you out of the kingdom, where then will that fast be of use to you?
Do you not see that the skilled keepers of racing horses, when they are awaiting the race, prepare them by keeping them short of food?
But you deliberately oppress yourself with satiety.
In this way you outdo even the beasts in gluttony, for a weighed-down belly is good not only not for running, but not even for sleep,
for one oppressed by the abundance of food cannot even rest, but suffers, turning to and fro [?] again and again.
Fasting is the guardian of infants, the purifier of youths, the one who makes the elderly honorable, for the aged are more honorable
when adorned with fasting. For women it is a fine adornment, for vigorous young men a bridle, the protector of spouses, the nurturer of virginity.
Such are its benefits for each one individually. But for all in common, see again how does it govern life among us?
How in an instant does it turn the whole city and the whole people to good order?
It quiets loud clamor, drives away tumult, and silences evil talk, like a teacher whose arrival in this way, in an instant, calms the uproar of children,
How, when the fast dawns, it silences all the tumult of the city!
What singer has come forth during a fast? What assembly of impurity has gathered because of a fast?
Wanton laughter, songs of fornication, and frenzied dances are at once driven out of the city; as if by some fierce judge, so are they expelled by the fast.
If all were to take it as the counselor of their affairs, nothing would prevent the whole world from living in deep peace;
nations would not rise up against one another, armies would not fight one another, and weapons would not be forged.
If fasting were firmly established among us, law courts would not assemble, no one would dwell in prisons,
and there would be no evildoers at all in the wastelands, nor slanderers in the cities, nor those who lie in wait on the seas.
If all were disciples of fasting, there would not be heard at all, as Job says, the voice of the tax collector.
If fasting had crowned our life, it would not be so full of much grief and sighing,
for it would have taught us not only to fast from foods, but also to flee from and estrange ourselves from all love of money, greed, and all wickedness.
And once such things as these had been removed from us, nothing would any longer prevent our life from passing in peace and without turmoil.
But now those who cast fasting aside and pursue luxury as if it were blessedness bring in that great multitude of evils and destroy even their own bodies.
Consider the difference in faces, how they appear to you today, in the evening, and again tomorrow:
today the faces are swollen, reddened, drenched with sweat, the eyes moist and brazen, unable to see well because of the fog within;
but tomorrow they are calm, dignified, adorned with their natural color,
full of good order and all wisdom, when not a single cause darkens the natural power within.
Fasting is the likeness of the angels, the companion of the righteous, that which makes human life honorable.
This made Moses a lawgiver; Samuel is the fruit of fasting; with fasting Hannah prayed to God and said:

"Adonai Lord, Eloi, Sabaoth, if you will indeed look upon your handmaid and give me a child, I will give him before you as an offering; he shall drink neither wine nor strong drink until the day of his death."

This raised the great Samson, and as long as it was with him, warriors fell by him in their thousands, the gates of cities were torn up by him, and lions could not withstand the strength of his hands.
But when drunkenness and fornication took hold of him, from then on he became a captive of his enemies, was deprived of his eyes, and became an object of mockery to the children of the foreigners.
Elijah by fasting shut the heavens for three years and six months.
For when he saw that great outrage was being born of satiety, he fittingly brought upon them an involuntary fast through hunger,
by which he halted the boundless spread of their sin; as with a strong medicine, by fasting he cut away the excess of evil.
Receive this [fast], you poor, as your fellow-dweller and table companion; you slaves, as the one who gives you rest from the many hardships of your service;
you rich, as your physician, healing the ailments of satiety, and as the one who makes the foods you have come to despise through satiety more desirable to you;
you who are sick, as the mother of health; you who are healthy, as the guardian of your health.
Ask physicians and they will tell you that gluttony is the worst thing of all.
For this reason those who are experienced use fasting to reduce the great fatness of the flesh, so that the body's natural strength may not be weakened by immoderate fatness.
For by deliberate deprivation they undo excess and fatness and bring about [?] lightness.
Thus the benefit that comes from it is found in every matter and extends to all things: houses, neighborhoods, nights, days, deserts and cities.
Now therefore let us splendidly receive the leader of such good things, in accordance with the love [?] of the Lord; [? not] with gloom, like the faithless, but let us display the joy of the spirit.
But I think that I do not need to plead so hard about tomorrow's fast as I do that no one should fall today into the evils of drunkenness.
For many take fasting upon themselves even for the sake of custom and in emulation of one another, but I am afraid of drunkenness, which lovers of pleasure hold like an ancestral inheritance.
For just as if they were setting out on a long journey, so some senseless people drink wine today on account of these holy days of fasting that are coming.
Who is so senseless as to be like the drunken, out of his wits, before he has even drunk? Do you not know that the belly does not keep what has been stored in it?
The belly is an untrustworthy guardian, a treasury that does not preserve: when much goes into it, it retains the harm that comes from it, but it does not keep what has been sent down into it.
Take care that you too do not come tomorrow straight from drunkenness, and hear the reading: "I have not chosen such a fast," said the Lord.
Why do you mix things that cannot be mixed? What kinship does fasting have with drunkenness?
What fellowship does wine-bibbing have with holiness? What union does the temple of God have with idols?
For those are the temple of God in whom the Spirit of God dwells, and those are the temple of idols who through drunkenness take in the filth of defilement.
This present day is the gate of the fasts, and whoever defiles himself before the gates is never worthy to enter into the Holy of Holies.
What slave would there be who wished to calm his angry master and yet set up his master's enemy as his helper?
Drunkenness is enmity toward God, and fasting is the beginning of repentance.
Now if you wish to come to God through confession, flee drunkenness, so that no worse punishment may come upon you.
Yet abstinence from foods alone is not in itself enough to be called fasting.
Rather, let us fast a good fast, one pleasing to God. True fasting is estrangement from all evils:
fasting of the tongue, restraint of anger, separation from desires, from evil-speaking, from lying, and from false swearing.
Separation from all these is true and pleasing fasting; such a fast is good.
But let us delight in the Lord through training in the divine words of the Spirit, through acquiring the works of life, and through every profitable teaching.
And let us guard ourselves against that spiritual want, concerning which the prophet says:
"The Lord will not let the souls of the righteous starve," and again he says: "I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread."
For he did not say this about visible bread, since he knew that the sons of the patriarch Jacob went down to Egypt for bread;
rather, he was speaking about spiritual food, by which our inner man is made perfect. So may that famine not come upon us,
which was spoken of concerning the Jews: "For behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will bring famine upon this land,
not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord." That righteous Judge brought this on for this reason:
because he saw their mind starved of the food of the teachings of truth, and the outer man fattened.
But as for us, throughout all these following days may the Holy Spirit nourish us with the table of morning and evening, and may no one willingly be shut out from that spiritual table.
Rather, let us all drink from that holy cup which Wisdom has mixed for us and set before us, equally for all,
as much as each one is able to receive and drink, for "she has mixed her cup and slaughtered her sacrifices."
This is the food of the perfect, whose senses have been trained to distinguish good from evil,
which may we be worthy to receive richly, and may we be made worthy of the joy of the heavenly bridal chamber through Christ Jesus
our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.
